---
title: Rust, TypeScript and HTTP references
description: Reference pages from a Rust crate, a TypeScript package or an OpenAPI document, and several references in one site.
order: 5.5
---

[The API reference](api.qmd) makes pages from Python code. smalldocs can also make reference pages for
a Rust crate, for a TypeScript package, and for an HTTP API that an OpenAPI document describes. The pages
look like the Python pages. Each entry has a heading, a link to its source, a code block, its
description and a table.

The key `language` in the `api` section chooses the kind of code:

| `language` | What smalldocs reads | What you install |
|---|---|---|
| `python` | The package, which smalldocs imports. It is the default | smalldocs, in the environment of the package |
| `rust` | The JSON that rustdoc writes | A nightly toolchain of Rust |
| `typescript` | The JSON that TypeDoc writes | Node, and the packages of the project |
| `openapi` | An OpenAPI document, in JSON or YAML | Nothing for a file. uv for a FastAPI app |

For Rust and TypeScript, smalldocs does not read the code itself. A tool of the language reads the code,
and it writes what it knows as JSON. smalldocs runs that tool, reads the JSON and writes the pages. The
tool writes its output into a temporary folder, outside the project.

smalldocs does not import Rust or TypeScript code, so it needs no Python environment of the project.
Run it with uvx, which runs a Python tool from PyPI in a temporary environment:

```bash
uvx smalldocs api build --dir docs
uvx smalldocs render docs
```

## The keys of every language

Each `api` section reads these keys, whatever its language:

| Key | What it does | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `language` | `python`, `rust`, `typescript` or `openapi` | `python` |
| `out` | The folder of the reference pages, from the folder of the project. It must be inside that folder | `api` |
| `root` | The root of the repository, from the folder of the project. A source link is the path of the file from here | See the list below the table |
| `source` | The address of the code. Each entry links to its line there | None: no links to the code |
| `check-shown` | `smalldocs api check` holds the code only to what the pages show. See [Check the comments](#check-the-comments) | Off |
| `linkify` | Names in backticks link to their entries. The top-level `linkify` wins over it. When `api` is a list, only the top-level `linkify` counts, and a `linkify` in a section is a warning | On |

The default of `root` depends on the language:

- **Python:** see [Turn on the reference](api.qmd#turn-on-the-reference).
- **Rust:** with `manifest`, the git repository that holds the crate. Without it, the folder of the
  project when that folder holds a `Cargo.toml`, a `package.json` or `.git`, and its parent otherwise.
- **TypeScript:** the git repository that holds the first entry point. Without one, the folder of the
  project when that folder holds a `Cargo.toml`, a `package.json` or `.git`, and its parent otherwise.
- **OpenAPI:** the folder of the project when that folder holds a `Cargo.toml`, a `package.json`, a
  `pyproject.toml` or `.git`, and its parent otherwise.

Each build runs the tool of the language, before it builds the pages. A preview watches the folder of
the site only. An edit to code outside that folder starts no new build; save a page of the site to start
one.

A section warns for each key that its language does not read. For example, `entry` in a Rust section
gives this warning:

```
the api section with out 'api': entry is not read for rust; it is for typescript
```

A warning fails `smalldocs render --strict`. `smalldocs api build` and `smalldocs api check` print it.

## A Rust crate

### Install a nightly toolchain

rustdoc writes JSON only with the option `-Z unstable-options`, and only a nightly toolchain takes it.
Install one with rustup:

```bash
rustup toolchain install nightly
```

The nightly toolchain does not replace your default toolchain. smalldocs runs
`cargo +nightly rustdoc`, which uses nightly for that one command. smalldocs never installs a toolchain
itself. If cargo or the toolchain is missing, the build stops, and the message says how to install it.

### Turn on the reference

```yaml
api:
  language: rust
  manifest: ../Cargo.toml     # the crate, from the folder of the project
  out: api
  source: https://github.com/me/mycrate/blob/main
```

| Key | What it does | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `manifest` | The `Cargo.toml` of the crate, from the folder of the project. In a workspace, name the `Cargo.toml` of one package | The `Cargo.toml` at `root` |
| `toolchain` | The toolchain that runs rustdoc. Write it as text, in quotes if it looks like a number | `nightly` |
| `private` | Document the private items too. Write `true` or `false` with no quotes | Off |

The format of rustdoc's JSON changes between nightly releases. smalldocs reads the formats 57 and 61.
If rustdoc writes another format, the build stops with the format that it found. Then pin a dated
nightly that writes one of them, such as `toolchain: nightly-2026-11-11`.

A crate with only a binary, such as one with `src/main.rs` and no `src/lib.rs`, has no public API. So
smalldocs documents all of its items, the private ones too.

rustdoc writes its output into a folder that only you can write, in the temporary folder of the computer. If cargo
changes the `Cargo.lock` of the project, smalldocs puts the file back as it was.

### Write the doc comments

A doc comment is a comment that the doc tool of a language reads. In Rust it starts with `///`, or with
`//!` for a module. Give each function a doc comment, each parameter a docment, and each return value a
`# Returns` section. A docment is the `//` comment on the line of a parameter:

```rust
/// Add two numbers.
///
/// # Returns
///
/// The sum.
pub fn add(a: i32,  // the first number
           b: i32,  // the second number
) -> i32 {
    a + b
}
```

Put each parameter on its own line. A comment on a line with two parameters documents neither, because
smalldocs cannot tell which one it is for.

rustfmt, the formatter of Rust, moves a comment after the `{` into the body of the function. So the
return value takes a `# Returns` section, which is the convention of Rust. A comment on the line of `->`
still counts, if rustfmt leaves it there. A function that returns nothing needs no `# Returns` section.

A `# Arguments` list in the doc comment also documents the parameters, one line for each, as jagt does:

```rust
/// Render an `AGENT_TASK v1` packet, with its delegation and safety blocks, as text for standard
/// output.
///
/// # Arguments
///
/// * `options` - what the packet holds
///
/// # Returns
///
/// The packet, from its start line to its end line, each line ending in a newline.
pub fn render_task_packet(options: &TaskRenderOptions) -> Result<String> {
```

A parameter can be a pattern that unpacks its argument, as the handlers of a web server often are:

```rust
/// Show one task.
///
/// # Arguments
///
/// * `state` - the shared state of the server
/// * `id` - the task's id, from the path
pub async fn task_detail(State(state): State<AppState>, Path(id): Path<String>) -> Html<String> {
```

The page shows the pattern as the source writes it, such as `State(state)`. A comment after it on its
line documents it, and so does an `# Arguments` line with a name it binds, such as `state`. rustdoc's JSON names such a parameter `__arg0` in an `async fn`, so smalldocs reads its name
from the source.

A `# Returns` section of one paragraph moves into the table of the function. A longer section, for
example one with a list or an example, stays in the doc comment. The table then shows its first
paragraph. A field of a struct and a variant of an enum take a `///` doc comment, or a `//` comment on
their line.

### What the pages show

smalldocs writes one page for each module, in folders that follow the modules of the crate:

- The root of the crate is `api/<crate>.qmd`, such as `api/mycrate.qmd`.
- A module that holds other modules is the `index.qmd` of its folder, such as `api/geo/index.qmd`.
- A module with no modules in it is a page of its own, such as `api/geo/plane.qmd`.
- `api/index.qmd` lists the pages, with the summary of the crate. Its title is "Reference".

Each heading names the kind of item, such as `## fn add` or `## struct Point`. A method is one level
down, as `### Point::distance`. The methods of an `impl` block are entries under their type. An
`impl` of a trait is a line, such as "Implements `Display`". An item that a module exports again with
`pub use` has one entry, on the page of the module that declares it.

A link in a doc comment, such as ``[`Point`]``, becomes a link to its entry. A name from another crate,
such as `std::fmt::Display`, links to the documentation of that crate.

## A TypeScript package

### Install Node

TypeDoc needs Node and the packages of the project. Install them in the folder of the TypeScript
project:

```bash
npm install
```

If the project has TypeDoc, in `node_modules/.bin/typedoc`, smalldocs runs it. Otherwise smalldocs runs
`npx --yes --package typedoc@0.28 typedoc`. npx is the tool of Node that runs a package, and it keeps
TypeDoc 0.28 in the cache of npm. If Node is missing, the build stops and says so.

### Turn on the reference

`entry` names the entry points, the files that a package exports from. Give one path, a list of paths
or a folder. The front end of cricsdb is an app with no index file, so its section names a folder:

```yaml
api:
  language: typescript
  entry: ../frontend/src
  tsconfig: ../frontend/tsconfig.app.json
  root: ..
  source: https://github.com/rahuldave/cricsdb/blob/main
  out: api
```

| Key | What it does | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `entry` | The entry points, from the folder of the project: one path, a list of paths, or a folder | None. A TypeScript section without it stops the build |
| `tsconfig` | The `tsconfig.json` that TypeDoc reads, from the folder of the project | The one that TypeDoc finds |

TypeDoc gives only what the entry points export, and it follows `export * from`. When `entry` is a
folder, every file in the folder is an entry point.

### Write the doc comments

A doc comment in TypeScript is a JSDoc comment, which starts with `/**`. Give each export a doc
comment, and each parameter and each return value a docment. In TypeScript, a docment is the `//`
comment on the line of a parameter. The comment on the line of the `)` or the `{` documents the return
value:

```ts
/** Add two numbers. */
export function add(a: number,      // the first number
                    b: number = 1,  // the second number
): number {                         // the sum
  return a + b;
}
```

Without a docment, smalldocs uses the `@param` and `@returns` tags of the doc comment. On a signature of
one line, a comment documents the return value, even when a parameter is on that line too.

The description of a file is its module comment. smalldocs reads it as TypeDoc does:

- A comment with `@module` or `@packageDocumentation` is the comment of the module.
- A comment right before a declaration is the comment of that declaration.
- The first comment of a file is the comment of the module when an import, a re-export, `"use client"`,
  another doc comment or the end of the file follows it.

A React component is a function with a capital name, which returns JSX and takes no parameter or one
object of props. Its table shows the fields of its props, with the comment of each field and the
default from the destructured props. A component needs no comment on its return value, because it
returns what it draws. A destructured parameter takes the tags `@param props.footer` or `@param footer`:

```ts
/**
 * A panel with a footer; its props join `PanelProps` and its own.
 * @param props.footer the words at the bottom
 */
export function FooterPanel({ title, wide = false, footer }: PanelProps & { footer?: string }): JSX.Element {
```

Put each field of an interface or a type on its own line. A comment on a line with two fields documents
neither of them.

### What the pages show

smalldocs writes one page for each file, in folders that follow the folders of the source:

- A file `src/components/Badge.tsx` gives the page `api/components/Badge.qmd`. A folder that holds
  every file, such as `src/`, is left out.
- An `index.ts` gives the page of its folder, such as `api/components/index.qmd`.
- A folder with no page of its own gets an `index.qmd` that lists its pages.

Each heading names the kind of item, such as `## class Rect` or `## interface Point`. A function has
its name only, such as `## add`. A method is one level down, as `### Rect.area`. A name from another
package has no link.

## An HTTP API

An OpenAPI document is a JSON or YAML file in a standard format, which describes an HTTP API. It has an
entry for each operation, and a schema for each kind of data. An operation is one method on one path,
such as `GET /api/players/{player_id}`. A schema is the shape of one kind of data, such as a player.
Most web frameworks can write the document.

smalldocs reads OpenAPI 3.0 and 3.1. It reads 3.2 as 3.1, with a warning. A Swagger 2.0 document stops
the build.

### Give the document

A section with `language: openapi` takes exactly one of three inputs:

| Key | What it is | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `file` | A JSON or YAML file, from the folder of the project | A framework that writes a file, such as `cargo openapi generate` of dropshot or `tsoa spec` |
| `command` | A command that prints the document on its standard output. It runs in `root`, with no shell. Give one line, or a list of words | A small program of the project that prints the document |
| `fastapi` | A FastAPI app, as `module:attribute`, as uvicorn names it | A FastAPI app |

```yaml
api:
  - language: openapi
    file: ../openapi/my-api.json
    out: http
  - language: openapi
    command: cargo run --quiet --bin openapi   # a binary that prints the document
    out: rust-http
```

The standard output of a command must hold only the document. So a command must send its notices to
standard error, as `cargo run --quiet` does. A command that fails stops the build, with its exit code
and the end of its standard error. The key `timeout` gives the seconds to wait, and it is 300 by
default. smalldocs writes nothing into the project, but the command can. For example, `cargo run`
writes into `target/`.

### A FastAPI app

With `fastapi`, smalldocs runs a short program of its own in the environment of the project. The program
imports the app, calls `app.openapi()` and adds the file and the line of each route. It never starts a
server. smalldocs runs the program with `uv run --frozen python`, in `root`, so `root` must be the folder
that the import of the app starts from. The option `--frozen` never changes `uv.lock`, but uv can still
install packages into the `.venv` of the project. The key `python` gives another command for Python,
such as `python: .venv/bin/python`.

Some apps add their routes only when the server starts, in their lifespan function. An import of such
an app gives a document with no operations, and the build stops. Then name the function that adds the
routes in `setup`. The program calls it with the app before it calls `app.openapi()`. cricsdb adds its
routers in this way:

```yaml
api:
  - language: openapi
    fastapi: api.app:app
    setup: api.routers:register_routers
    root: ..
    out: reference
    source: https://github.com/rahuldave/cricsdb/blob/main
```

The setup function can be an `async def` function. `setup` works only with `fastapi`, and with `file`
or `command` it is an error. A command can do its own setup in its program. If a step of the program
fails, the message names the step, such as `setup-import`, and gives the end of the traceback.

Each operation gets a link to the line of its route, when `source` is set. A decorator without
`functools.wraps` makes the link point at the code of the decorator. A route on a
`functools.partial` has no link. The schemas of FastAPI get no link.

A program of another producer can add the source link too. Give the operation or the schema the
extension `x-smalldocs-source`, with a `file` and a `line`. A relative `file` starts at `root`.

### What the pages show

An OpenAPI tag is a name that groups operations, such as `Players`. FastAPI takes it from `tags=` on a
route or a router.

- Each tag gets a page, such as `reference/players.qmd`. The pages keep the order of the document.
- The operations with no tag go on the page `default.qmd`.
- An operation with several tags has one entry, on the page of its first tag.
- The schemas are on the page `schemas.qmd`, and `index.qmd` lists the pages.

The heading of an operation is its method and its path. Under it, the entry shows the request in a
code block, the summary and the description. Then it gives a table of the parameters, the request
body and a table of the responses. A type that is a schema links to its entry on `schemas.qmd`.

The pages leave out callbacks, webhooks, links, security schemes, examples, `servers`, the headers of
responses, and limits on a value such as `maximum`.

## Several references in one site

`api` can be a list of sections. Each section names its `language` and has its own `out` folder:

```yaml
api:
  - packages: [cricsdb]         # python, the default language
    root: ..
    out: python
  - language: openapi
    fastapi: api.app:app
    root: ..
    out: reference
```

- **`out`** must differ for each section. Two sections with the same `out`, or one `out` inside another,
  stop the build.
- **`linkify`** is at the top level of the config for a list, or under `smalldocs:` in a `_quarto.yml`.
- **`--out NAME`** runs only the section whose `out` is `NAME`, as in
  `smalldocs api build --out reference --dir docs`.
- **`smalldocs api list` and `smalldocs api module`** are for Python only. With a list, they use its
  one Python section. With several Python sections, give `--out NAME`.

All the sections write their names into one `_symbols.json`. A name that two sections give links to the
first section. When two sections give the same full name, the build also warns. For example, a Python module
`reference` and an OpenAPI section with `out: reference` can both give `reference.Player`.

If you remove a section from the list, its pages stay, and the build warns with their folder. Remove
the folder yourself.

## The pages that a build writes

A build never writes over a page that a person wrote. A Rust, TypeScript or OpenAPI build marks each page
that it writes. The mark is the first line of the front matter:

```yaml
# written by smalldocs api build; a build writes over it
```

- A build writes over a page, or deletes it, only when the page has the mark, and when the manifest
  `out/.smalldocs-api` lists it.
- If a page of the build goes where a page without the mark is, the build stops. A page that you edited
  loses its mark, so remove the edited page, or move it.
- A folder index of your own, such as `api/components/index.qmd`, stays. The page of the module then
  goes beside it, as `api/components/components.qmd`.

A sidebar entry `auto: api/**` lists the pages in folders, as Quarto does. It makes no section for
`api` itself, and it leaves out `api/index.qmd`. Each folder in `api` is a section.

## Check the comments

`smalldocs api check` runs the tool of the language and reports each gap, one on a line. Its exit code
is 1 when it finds a gap. Here it runs on the small crate of the tests of smalldocs, with `--shown`:

```
tinycrate              26 of  32
tinycrate::shapes       2 of   2
tinycrate::geo          1 of   1
tinycrate::geo::plane   1 of   1
tinycrate::written      4 of   5
tinycrate::deep         1 of   1

tinycrate:scale: no return docment; write a `# Returns` section in its doc comment
tinycrate:undocumented: no doc comment
tinycrate:undocumented(x): no docment
tinycrate:undocumented: no return docment; write a `# Returns` section in its doc comment
tinycrate:Holder::new(v): no docment
tinycrate:Holder::new(v): no docment
tinycrate:apply: no return docment; write a `# Returns` section in its doc comment
tinycrate:Size.w: no docment
tinycrate:Size.h: no docment
tinycrate::written:read_quietly: no return docment; write a `# Returns` section in its doc comment
35 of 42 items are documented
```

Each line of the table gives a module, and how many of its items are documented. `Holder::new` is
there twice, because the crate has two `impl` blocks with a `new` each.

Each language holds the code to its own rules:

- **Rust:** each item needs a doc comment, each parameter a docment or an `# Arguments` line, and each
  return value a `# Returns` section. A field and a variant need a comment. Without `--shown` or
  `check-shown: true`, `check` also holds the private items.
- **TypeScript:** each file needs a module comment, and each export a doc comment. Each parameter and
  each return value that is not `void` needs a docment or a tag. TypeDoc gives only what the package
  exports, so `check` always holds only what the pages show.
- **OpenAPI:** each operation needs a summary or a description, and each parameter a description. Each
  schema and each of its fields needs a description. For a FastAPI app, an operation needs its
  description, which is the docstring of its function. FastAPI makes every summary from the name of the
  function. `check` also counts the parameters with no description by name.

A field of a type that has its own entry is reported once, at that entry, such as `Box.width`. A field
whose comment is on a line with other fields is reported with the reason.

With `check-responses: true` in an OpenAPI section, each `2xx` response also needs a schema. A `2xx`
response has a status from 200 to 299. A `204` response has no body, so `check` does not hold it. The
empty schema `{}` and an object with no fields count as no schema. FastAPI writes them for a route that
returns a plain `dict`, and a Pydantic `response_model` is the fix. The option is off by default.

`check` does not hold the schemas `HTTPValidationError` and `ValidationError`, which FastAPI adds
itself. With a list, `check` runs every section, and prints a line such as `api section reference
(openapi)` before each one.

## Link names from the text

On a site with a Rust, TypeScript or OpenAPI section, a name in backticks links when it is a key of
`_symbols.json`, letter for letter. A Python site also needs the name to look like code. So on these
sites `useFetch` and `GET /api/players/{player_id}` link to their entries. A name with the
class `nolink` stays as code, as on a Python site.

The keys of `_symbols.json` are these names:

| Language | The names |
|---|---|
| Rust | `Point`, `Point::distance`, `Point.distance` and `mycrate::Point::distance` |
| TypeScript | `add`, a member such as `Rect.moved`, and the name with its file, such as `components/Badge.Badge` |
| OpenAPI | The method and the path, such as `GET /api/players/{player_id}`. The `operationId`, such as `getPlayer`. The name of a schema, such as `Player`, and the name after `out`, such as `reference.Player` |

A name links only when it is the same text as a key. So in the narrative of an HTTP API, write each
path with the parameter names of the document. `GET /api/players/{id}` does not link to
`GET /api/players/{player_id}`.
